analysis.one_liner: Rewrites the Endangered Species Act to make it harder to list species and easier for developers and landowners to build and operate in protected habitat.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Resources Committee 25-15 and was placed on the House calendar in October 2000, but never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act to raise the bar for listing a species as endangered, give state governors and permit applicants new leverage over wildlife decisions, let agencies skip or walk away from the required wildlife consultations, cap the mitigation costs developers can be charged, and narrow the ability of citizens to sue to enforce the law. It was reported out of the House Resources Committee on a 25-15 vote but never reached the House floor, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries would be owners and users of land and water where endangered species live — real estate developers, homebuilders, agriculture, oil and gas, mining, timber, and electric utilities. The bill would make listing decisions harder to obtain and easier to challenge, let federal agencies proceed with projects if the wildlife agency misses a deadline, exempt routine operation of pipelines, dams, and power lines from consultation, bar most citizen suits that do not show immediate irreparable harm, cap mitigation costs for public projects at 10 percent, and forbid imposing new species protections on a permittee after a permit is issued. A secondary group that benefits: private landowners who could get up to $10,000 grants under new "safe harbor" habitat agreements [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, resource industries, and large landowners

how_it_helps.text: It would require agencies to prefer field-collected data over models and to meet new documentation standards before listing a species, addressing industry complaints that listings rested on uncertain projections [S2].

It would guarantee developers and permit applicants a set of protections — deadlines for permit decisions, a ceiling on required mitigation, and a promise of no new species conditions once a permit is issued [S2].
It would create 'safe harbor' agreements and grants of up to $10,000 to private landowners who restore habitat, a genuine incentive for voluntary conservation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on endangered and threatened species and their habitats, since fewer species would qualify for protection and existing protections would be easier to escape. Because the ESA depends on citizen enforcement, ordinary Americans would also lose a major tool for holding agencies and developers accountable; the public would bear any loss of species and ecosystem benefits, including those tied to recreation, fisheries, and functioning ecosystems [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Endangered species and the public that values them

drawbacks.text: The bill would have made it significantly harder to protect species: listing decisions would have had to disfavor computer modeling in favor of field data [S2], agencies could have proceeded with projects if a required biological opinion was not delivered by a deadline [S2], and consultation would no longer be required for routine operation and maintenance of pipelines, dams, flood control works, and power lines [S2], each of which can allow habitat damage to continue while a species is in decline.

It would have capped the mitigation a public project could be required to fund at 10 percent of project costs, meaning wildlife protection would absorb the shortfall when a project's impact was expensive to offset [S2].

Citizen enforcement would have been narrowed: citizens could sue the federal government only if the violation posed immediate and irreparable harm to the species, and economic intervenors could enter and influence those suits [S2].

A state governor could effectively block a listing within the state by submitting scientific evidence the listing was unwarranted, unless the federal agency could disprove it by a preponderance of the evidence — a shifting of scientific authority toward state officials accountable to in-state industries [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's few genuine improvements — safe harbor agreements, a recovery-planning office, grant money for cooperating landowners — came bundled with provisions that would have sharply weakened the core protections of the Endangered Species Act: harder listings, gubernatorial vetoes by evidence, guaranteed exits from consultation, capped mitigation, and narrowed citizen enforcement. The good parts could be enacted alone; bundled this way, the trade was protection of imperiled species for lower costs and litigation risk for developers and resource industries. On balance the costs to wildlife and to the public's interest in functioning environmental safeguards outweighed the administrative improvements.

outcome.mechanism: The House Resources Committee approved the bill on a 25-15 party-line vote and placed it on the House calendar in October 2000, but leadership never brought it to the floor, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on October 27, 1999; it was referred to the House Committee on Resources, which he chaired [S1].
The committee held hearings in February and March 2000, marked the bill up on June 21, 2000, and ordered it reported by a vote of 25 to 15 [S5].
On October 26, 2000, the committee reported the bill (H. Rept. 106-1013) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting a House floor vote [S5].
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered species and the existing protections of the Endangered Species Act came out ahead, since the weakening bill never became law; landowners and developers gained nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Endangered species and existing wildlife protections

industries.note: The bill would cap required mitigation for public projects at 10 percent of project costs, add permitting deadlines, and forbid new species restrictions on permitted land without the owner's consent, lowering the cost and risk of building on habitat. The land-use burdens of listing decisions would shrink substantially [S2].

industries.industry: Oil, gas, mining, and timber interests
industries.note: Routine operation and maintenance of pipelines, flood control facilities, and power lines would be exempt from endangered species consultation, and agencies could proceed with actions if the wildlife agency missed deadlines for a biological opinion. Extractive users of federal land would also benefit from near-automatic national security exemptions from the Act [S2].

Maintenance and repair of irrigation, drainage, and water conveyance structures would be excluded from the definition of a 'taking' of a protected species, and state governors could contest listings affecting land in their states. Farmers and water users would face fewer restrictions on irrigation and water projects [S2].
Contractors would gain faster permit timelines and a hard cap on mitigation spending, but public projects they build would bear the cost trade-off of reduced habitat protections [S2].

Every major protection mechanism of the existing law — listing standards, consultation, the take prohibition, citizen suits, critical habitat designation — would be narrowed. Species with the least commercial constituency would have the least chance of protection [S2].
